definition: The Gaussian distribution, often called the normal distribution, is an extremely common continuous probability distribution—a function that tells the probability of a number in some context falling between any two real numbers.
details: The Gaussian distribution, often called the normal distribution, is an extremely common continuous probability distribution—a function that tells the probability of a number in some context falling between any two real numbers.

explainer.lead: The Gaussian, or normal, distribution is a common way to describe continuous values that cluster around an average. Its importance comes from turning that pattern into probabilities: it can estimate how likely a value is to fall within any chosen interval.

tiers.eli5: Imagine measuring the heights of many similar plants. Most heights sit near the middle, while very short and very tall plants are less common. A Gaussian distribution is a smooth mathematical curve for this pattern, and the area under part of the curve tells you how likely a height in that range is.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use Gaussians to model continuous noise, initialize probabilistic models, and calculate interval probabilities through the density and cumulative distribution functions. Libraries such as NumPy and SciPy support sampling and these calculations, using a mean and a positive standard deviation. A common pitfall is assuming data are Gaussian without checking, especially when they are skewed, bounded, or contain heavy tails.
tiers.paperLevel: For mean μ and standard deviation σ > 0, the probability density is f(x) = exp(-(x-μ)^2/(2σ^2)) / (σ sqrt(2π)). The probability of an interval is the integral of this density over that interval; the density itself is not a probability. The distribution is symmetric about μ and has support over all real numbers, so it may be unsuitable for bounded, skewed, or heavy-tailed data.

explainer.example: For the standard Gaussian, μ = 0 and σ = 1. The probability that a value lies between -1 and 1 is approximately 0.683, meaning the model assigns about 68.3% of the probability to that interval.

explainer.intuition: Picture a smooth curve whose area represents probability. Values near the center are typical under the model, and the area between any two points gives the probability of landing in that range.
howItWorks: Choose a mean μ, which sets the center of the distribution.
Choose a positive standard deviation σ, which controls its spread.
Evaluate the Gaussian density to describe the relative shape across real values.
Integrate the density from a to b to obtain P(a ≤ X ≤ b).
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives a compact two-parameter model for continuous uncertainty and a precise way to turn a range of values into a probability. This makes it a basic building block for statistical and probabilistic reasoning.
misconceptions: A Gaussian density value is not itself the probability of that exact value; probabilities come from areas over intervals.
Not every dataset with a central peak is Gaussian, so symmetry and tail behavior also matter.
A Gaussian is not always centered at zero; its mean can be any real number.
